Chapter 3: How Policy and Culture Reinforce Inequality
Picture yourself strolling down the halls of a public school. You can almost feel how policy and culture shape every corner of daily life. Some classrooms buzz with new books and eager faces, while others are weighed down by broken equipment and low spirits. And you know what? These differences aren’t just random. They come from decisions made over years—decisions that really show what people believe about who deserves what.
Think about a principal, juggling a tight budget. They’re faced with impossible choices. Should they put more money into the science lab, or save the arts program? Who gets extra support? These decisions aren’t just about numbers—they’re shaped by policies set far away, by folks who may never even step foot in the school. And underneath it all, there’s the culture of the community: what people value, what they hope for, and sometimes, what they’re afraid of.
This dance between policy and culture is really at the core of how inequality sticks around. Laws and rules set the boundaries, but it’s culture that fills in the details—teaching everyone what’s “normal” and what’s not. Maybe a city decides to build a new highway. But the route they pick? It often slices through certain neighborhoods, making it harder for some folks to get to work or school. Or take a company’s hiring standards—they might look neutral, but often they're shaped by old ideas about who’s truly “qualified.”
The tricky part? Most of us don’t even notice these patterns, because they’re just so familiar. A parent might shrug off their child’s underfunded school, thinking that’s just how it goes. An employee might accept that promotions only go to a certain kind of person, believing it’s just the way things are. But here’s something to pay attention to—these patterns aren’t natural. They’re the result of choices, guided by beliefs about whose lives matter most.
Over time, all these choices add up. We end up with a society where opportunity isn’t spread evenly. Some people get access to good jobs, safe neighborhoods, and quality healthcare—while others are left behind. The gap between rich and poor keeps growing, and that sense of shared purpose? It starts to fade away.
And it’s not just the most disadvantaged who feel the impact. When whole communities are cut off from opportunity, everyone loses. Businesses have fewer talented people to hire. Public services get stretched thin. Social trust starts to crumble. Suddenly, instead of feeling like we’re all in it together, people start looking at each other with suspicion or resentment.
Culture, in all its forms, is a powerful force in keeping these systems going. The stories we tell, the symbols we use, and the rituals we repeat—they all shape what people expect from themselves and from others. When the media paints certain groups as dangerous or lazy, those images sink in and affect real lives. And when history books skip over the contributions of entire communities, we all miss out on what’s possible.
But here’s the hopeful part: culture isn’t just something that holds us back. It can be a spark for change. When people share new stories, celebrate new heroes, or dream up new possibilities, what seems “acceptable” begins to shift. Imagine students pushing for a more inclusive curriculum, or a company rethinking the way it hires. Maybe a neighborhood comes together to protect its history. These small acts of resistance start to chip away at old patterns—and open the door to something better.
The relationship between policy and culture? It’s not set in stone. It’s shaped by the choices we all make, every single day. By noticing how rules and expectations reinforce inequality—and daring to imagine new ways of living together—we can start building a society where everyone gets a real chance to thrive.
